book_unit: Unit 7 - Selfies / Wrong name, wrong place
grammar_topic: past simple of be: was / were
title: The Photo from 1985
body: Last month my father was in the attic of our old house. There were many boxes there, and in one box there was a photo. In the photo, there were two young men in front of our house. 'Who were they?' I asked. 'The one on the left was my father — your grandfather,' Dad said. 'But who was the other man? I don't know.' We were curious. The photo was from 1985 — the year was on the back. We showed the photo to our oldest neighbour. She was quiet for a minute. Then she smiled: 'Oh! That was Anvar, your grandfather's best friend. They were students together. He was funny and kind. His family was from Khorog, and after university he was a teacher there.' That evening, Dad found Anvar's son online. Now our families are friends again — because of one old photo. The attic wasn't just a room with boxes. It was a door to the past.

book_unit: Unit 7 - Selfies / Wrong name, wrong place
grammar_topic: past simple: regular and irregular verbs
title: The Wrong Wedding
body: Last Saturday, my friend Behruz received an invitation: 'Wedding of Firdavs and Madina, Restaurant Gulistan, 6 p.m.' He bought a nice present, put on his best suit and went to the restaurant. The music played, people danced, and Behruz enjoyed the party. He ate plov, talked to the guests and congratulated the groom's father. After two hours, he wanted to give his present to the happy couple. He walked to their table and stopped. The groom wasn't Firdavs! Behruz looked around. He didn't know these people! Then he checked the invitation and understood everything. Restaurant Gulistan had two halls. The wedding of HIS friends was in the second hall! Behruz laughed, said sorry to everyone and moved to the right hall. He arrived just in time for the cake. Later he told his friends the story. Firdavs laughed the most: 'You danced for two hours at a stranger's wedding — and nobody asked you anything?' 'People are friendly at weddings,' Behruz answered. 'Everyone thought I was a cousin!'

book_unit: Unit 8 - A murder mystery / A house with a history
title: Who Ate the Cake?
body: Yesterday was my mother's birthday, and I made a chocolate cake for her. I finished it at three o'clock and left it on the kitchen table. At five o'clock, I came back — and saw only an empty plate! Who ate the cake? There were four people at home. I started my investigation. First, I asked my sister. 'I didn't eat it,' she said. 'I was at my music lesson. I came home at half past four.' Then I asked my father. 'I didn't do it,' he said. 'I watched football in the living room all afternoon.' My little brother said: 'I don't like chocolate.' That wasn't true — but he had no chocolate on his face, and his hands were clean. Then I heard a strange sound under the table. Our cat Barsik didn't look at me. There was chocolate cream on his white nose. 'Barsik! Cats can't eat chocolate — it's dangerous!' We called the vet, but Barsik was fine. He ate only the cream. The cake itself was on the floor behind the door. My investigation found two things: a guilty cat and a very dirty kitchen.

book_unit: Unit 8 - A murder mystery / A house with a history
title: The House on Green Street
body: There is an old house on Green Street, and children tell scary stories about it. 'There was a rich man there a hundred years ago,' they say. 'And now there are ghosts!' Last week, my friends and I decided to check. In the morning, we opened the old gate and went in. Inside, there was a lot of dust and there were spiders on the walls. But there weren't any ghosts. There was a big library with hundreds of old books. There was a piano — very old, but beautiful. And there was a photo on the wall: a man with kind eyes, and children around him. Our teacher explained everything at school: 'That man was a doctor. There was a free hospital for poor children in his house. He wasn't rich at the end of his life — he spent all his money on medicine for them.' Now there is a plan in our town: to make a museum in the house. There aren't any ghosts on Green Street. There is only a good story that people forgot.

title: Osh for Twenty People
body: On Sunday my uncle cooks osh for the whole family — about twenty people. In the morning we go to the market together. 'How much rice do we need?' I ask. 'Three kilos,' he says. 'And a lot of carrots — two kilos, and some good meat.' At the market, there is a mountain of yellow carrots. My uncle checks them carefully. 'Not these. Those are better.' We buy some oil, a few onions and a little garlic. 'How many onions?' — 'Five or six. And how much salt? Nobody knows — the hand knows!' At home, my uncle starts the fire. First the oil, then the meat, then the onions and the carrots. The smell is fantastic. He adds the rice and some water. 'Now we wait. Don't touch it! Don't open it!' After an hour, the osh is ready. There isn't much talk at the table — everyone is busy. 'Uncle, how much osh is left?' my cousin asks after lunch. My uncle looks into the big pot and laughs: 'Not much. Only a little — for breakfast!'

title: The Melon Championship
body: Every August, our village has a small championship: whose melon is the best? My father takes it very seriously. 'My melons are sweeter than Rustam's,' he says every year. 'And bigger. And rounder.' This year, his main melon was truly enormous — heavier than our cat and bigger than a football. Father was happier than a child. On the day of the competition, the judges walked from table to table. Rustam's melon was beautiful, but smaller. Our neighbour's melon was big, but paler. Father smiled. And then came Grandmother Zulfiya, eighty years old, with a melon on a little cart. Her melon was... not very big. Not very round. But the judges cut it, tried one piece — and their faces changed. It was sweeter than honey. 'Size is important,' said the main judge, 'but taste is more important.' Grandmother Zulfiya took the first prize. My father took the second. Now he says: 'Next year my melon is going to be bigger AND sweeter. I have a secret plan.' We'll see. In our village, the melon championship is more serious than football.

book_unit: Unit 10 - The most dangerous place / Five continents in a day
title: The Highest Road
body: My cousin Daler is a driver, and his route is one of the highest roads in the world — the Pamir Highway. Last summer he took me with him. 'This is the most beautiful office on Earth,' he said and started the engine. The first day was easy. But then the road climbed higher and higher. The mountains were the biggest things I have ever seen. The air became thinner, and my head felt strange. 'Drink more water,' Daler said. 'It's the best medicine here.' We stopped in a small village for the night. It was the quietest place in the world — no cars, no internet, only stars. An old man gave us bread and tea. 'You have the most difficult job,' I said to Daler in the morning. He shook his head: 'No. I have the most interesting one. Every week I see the highest mountains, the cleanest lakes and the kindest people in the country. What is difficult about that?' I looked at the white peaks around us and agreed. Sometimes the hardest roads go to the most wonderful places.

book_unit: Unit 10 - The most dangerous place / Five continents in a day
title: Big Plans
body: It's the last evening of the school year, and my friends and I are sitting on the roof of my house. The city lights are below us, and our future is in front of us. 'What are you going to do after school?' asks Jamshed. Everyone has a plan. 'I'm going to study medicine in Dushanbe,' says Nigora. 'I'm going to be a doctor like my mother.' 'I'm going to open a small computer club,' says Jamshed. 'Kids are going to learn programming there.' Aziz is quiet for a minute. 'You're going to laugh,' he says, 'but I'm going to be a chef. I'm going to cook the best osh in the country, and my restaurant is going to be famous.' Nobody laughs. His plov is already the best in our street. 'And you?' they ask me. I look at the stars. 'I'm going to travel,' I say. 'First Samarkand, then Istanbul, then the world. And one day I'm going to write a book about it.' 'It's going to be a boring book,' Jamshed jokes, 'without a chapter about my computer club!' We laugh, but I know: we're going to remember this evening for a long time.

book_unit: Unit 11 - Culture shock / Experiences or things?
grammar_topic: adverbs of manner; verb + to + infinitive
title: Learning to Drive
body: Last month I decided to learn to drive. My teacher, Mr Nazarov, is a calm man with thirty years of experience. On our first lesson, he spoke slowly and clearly: 'Rule number one: drive carefully. Rule number two: think quickly, but decide calmly.' I started the car nervously. It moved... backwards. 'Interesting choice,' Mr Nazarov said quietly. 'Most students want to go forwards.' Week after week, I learned to drive better. I stopped smoothly at traffic lights, turned correctly and parked... well, I tried to park. Parking was my enemy. 'You need to feel the car,' my teacher explained patiently. 'Don't fight it.' Yesterday was my exam. I drove slowly and carefully. The inspector nodded and wrote something. Then came the parking. I breathed deeply, turned the wheel gently — and the car entered the space perfectly. 'Congratulations,' the inspector said. I wanted to dance happily on the street. Mr Nazarov shook my hand warmly: 'Remember: a good driver never stops learning.'

book_unit: Unit 11 - Culture shock / Experiences or things?
title: Presents or Memories?
body: My aunt Mavluda lives in Canada, and every year she sends us money for New Year. 'Buy something nice,' she writes. Last year my brother bought a phone. I bought clothes. This year, our mother had a different idea. 'Things break and get old,' she said. 'Let's buy an experience.' So we bought four tickets to the mountains — for the whole family. We stayed in a small guest house near a lake. In the mornings we walked in the forest. In the evenings we played games and drank tea with honey. My brother forgot about the internet — there wasn't any! On the last day, we sent Aunt Mavluda a photo: four happy faces, white mountains, golden sun. She answered quickly: 'This is the best present in years! Next December I'm going to come, and we're going to go together.' My old phone still works. My clothes from last year are still fine. But those three days in the mountains? They are going to stay with me forever. Mum was right: things get old, memories don't.

book_unit: Unit 12 - I've seen it ten times! / He's been everywhere!
title: The Film Expert
body: My friend Sino is a film expert. At least, he thinks so. 'Have you seen this film?' — this is his favourite question. He has seen everything. 'I've watched all the famous films,' he says proudly. 'I've seen the old ones and the new ones. I've watched films from ten different countries.' Last Friday our teacher started a film club at school. The first film was a classic — a black-and-white comedy from the 1960s. 'Ah, this one!' Sino said loudly. 'I've seen it ten times! It's brilliant!' The film started. After twenty minutes, Sino looked confused. After forty minutes, he was completely quiet. The film was in French — and the ending was sad, not funny. 'Sino,' I whispered, 'have you really seen this film?' He was red like a tomato. 'I've... seen the poster,' he said. 'Many times. In my film book.' The class laughed for five minutes. Sino is still our film expert. But now he has a new rule: 'Never say you've seen a film... before you've actually watched it.'

book_unit: Unit 12 - I've seen it ten times! / He's been everywhere!
title: Grandfather's Map
body: My grandfather has a big map on his wall, with small red pins on it. Each pin is a place he has visited. 'I've been to eleven countries,' he told me yesterday. 'Have you ever been to India?' I asked. 'Yes, I have. I went there in 1979, when I was a young engineer. We built a power station. The heat was unbelievable!' 'And China?' 'I've been there twice. The first time was in 1985. The second time was last year — your uncle took me. Everything has changed! In 1985 everyone rode bicycles. Now the cities are full of electric cars.' I looked at the map. 'Which country have you loved the most?' Grandfather smiled and put his finger on Tajikistan. 'I've seen beautiful places, but I've never found a better one than home. Travel, my dear. See the world. And then you'll understand me.' Yesterday I bought my own map. It has one pin so far — our town. But I've already made a list: Samarkand, Almaty, Istanbul... My journey has just started.
